rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: CAA winter-flying guidance covers aircraft preparation, contaminated surfaces and flight in icing conditions.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: Operators must establish procedures for flights in expected or actual icing conditions where required by the operating rules.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: A pilot should only commence or intentionally continue into expected or actual icing when the aircraft is certified and equipped for those conditions.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: If icing exceeds the aircraft's certification capability, the pilot should leave the icing conditions without delay.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: Take-off should not begin when ice or other deposits could adversely affect aircraft performance or controllability.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: Complex-aircraft operations require ground de-icing, anti-icing and associated inspection procedures when needed.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: The clean-aircraft principle requires frost, ice and other contamination to be removed before flight.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: Winter checks should consider pitot-static contamination, water in fuel, carburettor icing and changing weather conditions.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: Aircraft-icing risk depends on aircraft certification, cloud and precipitation, temperature, contamination, flight phase, equipment, procedures and crew decisions.

rows.source: CAA aircraft icing and winter-operation safety
rows.verified: CAA icing evidence is aircraft-, operation-, weather-, contamination-, crew- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: ORR is the enforcing authority for level crossings in Great Britain.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Railway businesses must manage level-crossing risk through their safety-management systems.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: ORR provides assurance and can take enforcement action where a crossing is not being made safe.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Risk should be reduced through crossing design or an alternative method of crossing where reasonably practicable.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Risk assessment should consider how a crossing is actually used rather than relying only on its intended use.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Level-crossing assessments should be completed by competent people who understand hazards, controls and user behaviour.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Effective risk management requires cooperation among infrastructure managers, operators, local authorities, highways authorities and users.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: ORR reports just under 5,500 level crossings on the mainline network and an estimated 1,500 on heritage and minor railways.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Level-crossing risk depends on crossing type, train frequency and speed, road or pedestrian use, visibility, behaviour, controls and maintenance.

rows.source: ORR level-crossing risk management
rows.verified: Level-crossing evidence is crossing-, route-, user-, traffic-, control- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision probability.
